title: The Side Experiment That Outgrew Nupedia in January 2001
dek: An expert-reviewed encyclopedia with about two dozen finished articles tried an open wiki on the side, and the two men behind it still disagree about the credit.

story.event: Launching an open wiki beside the slow, expert-reviewed Nupedia
story.summary: Nupedia, a free online encyclopedia funded by Jimmy Wales's company Bomis and edited by Larry Sanger, had finished only about two dozen articles under a seven-step expert review by early 2001. After learning about wikis, Sanger proposed one to the Nupedia list on 10 January 2001; when most of Nupedia's advisory board objected, it relaunched on its own domain as Wikipedia on 15 January and grew far faster. Wales and Sanger have since disagreed over whether Sanger was a co-founder.
paragraphs: Early in 2000 Jimmy Wales hired a philosopher, Larry Sanger, to run Nupedia, a free online encyclopedia paid for entirely, Sanger later wrote, by Bomis, the San Diego internet company Wales co-owned. To be taken seriously, Wales later said, it had to be even more academic than a printed encyclopedia, so every article passed through a seven-step expert review. By the winter of 2000 to 2001, by Sanger's count, about 25 articles had been approved. Wales recalled starting a short biography of the economist Robert Merton himself and feeling as intimidated as in "the bad part of grad school".

On 2 January 2001 Sanger had dinner at a Mexican restaurant in Pacific Beach with Ben Kovitz, who explained wikis: web pages anyone could edit. Wales has said a Bomis employee, Jeremy Rosenfeld, had shown him the idea the month before. On 10 January Sanger put it to Nupedia's mailing list: "No, this is not an indecent proposal." Wales, he told the list, thought many people might find it objectionable; Sanger thought not. He offered it as a low-risk experiment, kept apart from Nupedia and clearly labelled, so its quality would not reflect on the main site. That evening it was running: "Told you we could make it fast."

A clear majority of Nupedia's advisory board, Sanger wrote, wanted nothing to do with a wiki. Wales remembered the worry that the academics would hate it, and the decision to treat it as a side project rather than convert Nupedia. On 15 January it relaunched on its own domain as Wikipedia, a name Sanger says he coined. Sanger counted about 600 articles by the end of January and 3,900 by May; Wales later said they got more done in two weeks than Nupedia had managed since it began.

Bomis was losing money in the dot-com slump, and Sanger was laid off in early 2002. The two men have disagreed ever since over who founded what. Sanger has written that the encyclopedia idea and the funding were entirely Wales's, and that applying wiki software to it was his. Wales has called Sanger a subordinate employee and, in 2007, his co-founder claim "absurd"; in 2023 he said Sanger "doesn't get enough credit for his early work", while rejecting the title.

quote.text: It is contrary to sound judgment, and repugnant to the maxims of the prudent, to take a medicine on conjecture, or to follow a road but in the track of the caravan.
quote.locator: Chapter VIII, "Of the Duties of Society", maxim XC
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: Saadi states the advisory board's case: do not take medicine on guesswork, keep to the caravan's track. Wikipedia left the track and grew far beyond Nupedia, yet Saadi's question, who has checked what you are about to swallow, did not go away when the articles multiplied.

reflection: Two things in this story sit uneasily together, and both are worth keeping. A careful system produced very little, while a cheap experiment, fenced off so it could fail quietly, produced more in weeks than the careful one had in months. And Saadi is still right that guesswork is no way to take medicine; some work does need the slow review.

The other thread is credit. Two people who built something together have spent two decades disagreeing about what to call each other. Whoever you are working with, it is kinder to say plainly and early who is doing what, before success makes the question matter.
invitation: Name one thing you are holding back for a full review that could be tried as a small, clearly labelled experiment instead. Tell one colleague today what the experiment is and how you would know it had failed.

research_notes: Founding credit is disputed and both views are given, attributed. Sanger (Slashdot memoir, 2005) credits Wales with the original idea of a free encyclopedia and with all the funding through Bomis, and claims for himself the idea of adapting wiki software to it, the name and much early organising. Wales (AP, 2007) called Sanger a subordinate employee and his co-founder claim 'absurd'; in 2005 (wikipedia-l) and 2023 (Lex Fridman) he said Jeremy Rosenfeld, a Bomis employee, had shown him the wiki concept in December 2000, before Sanger raised it; in 2023 he also said Sanger does not get enough credit for his early work but that co-founder is not the right title. Sanger's memoir records Wales as liking the idea but being initially sceptical; Sanger's 10 January post says Wales thought many might find it objectionable. AP notes that early press releases described both as founders, which Sanger says Wales approved and Wales disputes; the story does not adjudicate. Nupedia's output: Sanger gives about 25 approved articles by early winter 2001 in the memoir and elsewhere 'just over 20' after 18 months; the story uses about 25, attributed. Wales says Nupedia started about two years before Wikipedia and that more was done in two weeks than in almost two years, but Nupedia began in early 2000 (memoir; Meta timeline), so the story paraphrases him as 'than Nupedia had managed since it began'. Wikipedia's early article counts are Sanger's and are attributed. Funding: in 2001 both projects were paid for by Bomis, Wales's privately held company, with volunteer writers, so funding is recorded as bootstrapped rather than the slate's nonprofit; the Wikimedia Foundation came later and is not part of the episode. The Saadi maxim is general advice on prudence, applied here by analogy to the advisory board's objection.
